The Mulshine Family Menu Tree Book

The Stone and the Rose

the Mulshine family's journey, from Castletownroche to the world
told from the family history researched and written by John Mulshine
— for his children, and their children, to add down the road —
scroll ↓
I · The Town on the Awbeg

Castletownroche, County Cork

The story begins in a village above a river bend — Castletownroche, where the Roches raised their castle in the fourteenth century, where Cromwell's men hanged Lady Ellen Roche for defending it in 1650, and where the mill wheels turned on the Awbeg for centuries after.

In the parish register kept here from 1811, in a spidery clerical hand, live the earliest Mulshines we can name — though not yet by that spelling. The register says Mulchinach. Older still, the Irish: Ó Maoilsionóg.

The name would not settle into “Mulshine” until New York.

The book: town history pp. 177–180, county map p. 201 · digital edition
II · 20 May 1817

Patrick & Margaret

On the twentieth of May, 1817, Patrick Mulchinach married Margaret Flemming at Castletownroche — Richard Flemming and Johanna Mulchinag standing witness. Every Mulshine in this story descends from that day.

Six children followed in the register: Denis, Moses, Michael, John, Patrick, and Margaret — whose 1837 baptism entry, No. 20 in the November register, is boxed by hand in the copy John keeps: his great-great-aunt, found in the ink.

By Griffith's Valuation of 1850, Patrick held a house and yard on New Road. His neighbors were named Roche.

“Did they know each other in Castletownroche....most likely.” — John, on the family that would give his great-grandfather a wife
The book: marriage record p. 14, the boxed baptism p. 15, Griffith's Valuation p. 19
III · 1845–1849

The Crossing

Denis went first, in 1845 — before the worst of the Famine, before Ellis Island existed. By 1850 he was living at 125 Allen Street in the Five Points, the hardest square mile in America. A stone mason. The census taker's margin note beside his name, a century later, reads simply: “1st Mulshine in U.S.”

Moses followed on the Arcola in March 1849. And that same year came Michael, eighteen years old, who moved in with Denis and Hannah's family and would become John's great-grandfather.

It took John thirty years of searching to find Denis.

“I actually cried a little... I am probably the only person in more than a century to feel this depth of emotion for Denis and Hannah.” — John, on the discovery

They endured the years of “No Irish Need Apply.” Of the twenty-eight children born to these families in New York, John counts eleven who lived past the age of nine. The hand-drawn map of the family plots at Calvary Cemetery — behind this page — is where most of them rest.

The book: Denis & Hannah pp. 40–50, the Calvary map p. 168
IV · The Stone Mason

Michael & Mary

In 1854, in Manhattan, Michael Mulshine married Mary Roche — baptized in the same Castletownroche parish, three years apart. Two children of one Irish village, finding each other across an ocean.

Michael cut stone. He swore his citizenship oath in 1855. They had four children: Noah, Dennis, Moses John, and little Margaret — who died in 1862, the same year as her mother. Mary was thirty-four.

“I assume Michael was a heavy drinker, as his son, Moses, was said to be a teetotaler due to the fact that his father drank too much.” — John, in the honest way of this book

Michael worked stone until pneumonia took him in January 1898, at 166 East 105th Street. The family remembered the ninth; the certificate says the tenth. The book keeps both, because that is what an honest family record does.

The book: Michael's chapter pp. 20–25, the death certificate p. 24
V · 1877

Dennis Sails for Australia

Michael's second son Dennis, a twenty-year-old bricklayer, boarded the N. Boynton in New York in February 1877 — the first ship of an “assisted immigrant policy” luring American tradesmen to New South Wales. He arrived at Port Jackson on 22 May. A newspaper artist sketched the ship coming in; John found the sketch, and beside it wrote: “Dennis Mulshine was on this ship for its arrival in Australia.”

The immigration ledger survives too, and one row of it is bracketed in John's hand: Mulshine, Denis, 20, Bricklayer, New York, R.C.

Dennis settled in Richmond, Victoria, married Janet Smith, and raised seven children. His daughter Vera married Frank Whelan at St Joseph's, Malvern, in 1920. When Clarrie — the last of the Australian sons — died in 1969, John writes, “our Mulshine direct blood line to Australia died as well.”

“When you are investigating your ancestry often times you hit walls. Occasionally, you stumble on gold.” — John, on finding the ledger
The book: the voyage pp. 126–135, the family albums pp. 116–124
VI · Second Avenue

Moses John, the Mayor

Michael's son Moses John Mulshine — grocer's clerk, fruit designer, teetotaler — was known in family lore as the Mayor of Second Avenue. In 1886 he married Margaret Mary Madden, daughter of Owen Madden of Kilbarry, Cork, and Ellen Falvey — nine Madden children in nineteen years.

Moses and Margaret raised their family through the tenement years, and buried too many of it: Eugene, Helen, little Margarit, an infant Moses, Joseph.

“It is family lore that this death broke Moses' heart. He tried to keep her alive by waking her in the middle of the night and taking her out of the tenements for fresh air.” — John, on five-year-old Margarit, 1901

Six children grew up: Michael Aloysius, Molly, Agnes, Eileen, Loretta — and Vincent, John's father. Moses died of asthma in 1913, and Second Avenue lost its mayor.

The book: Moses & Margaret pp. 51–62; the studio portrait behind this page is kept at p. 55
VII · The Other River

Wire, a Bridge, and a Broken Heart

John's mother's people were the Haighs — and their story out-Dickenses Dickens. Dudley Haley, the Fulton Market fish merchant, married his daughter Eliza to a dashing wire manufacturer named J. Lloyd Haigh, whose Brooklyn mills won the contract for the Brooklyn Bridge's cable wire.

Washington Roebling himself exposed Haigh for substituting rejected wire. In 1880 he went to Sing Sing for forgery. There had already been the singer, Jennie Hughes, and the bought-out theatre boxes, and the bigamy scandal in every paper. Years later, the man once among Brooklyn's richest was arrested for stealing an eight-cent loaf of bread.

Eliza never wavered — “she never uttered a word of complaint or reproach,” wrote the papers — and died in January 1881, days after her seventh child came, of what they called a broken heart. The warden could not release her husband for the funeral.

“It would be interesting to sit down with Steven Spielberg and lay out the life of Joseph Lloyd Haigh. There's got to be a time piece movie there!” — John

Their son Robert Dudley Haigh — photographed here in a workshop doorway — became a fireman-engineer, and the father of Dorothy.

The book: the Haigh chapters pp. 32–39 and 83–100; Eliza's obituary p. 38
VIII · Deep Roots

Charlemagne, and the Mayflower

In the 1940s, a St. John's University professor traced the Haigh line for the family — and kept going. Forty-one numbered generations from “Charlemagne, Emperor of the West, born A.D. 742” down through kings of France, dukes of Lorraine, earls of Arundel, the Gallups of Groton, and the Haleys of the fish market, to the Mulshine children.

And an eleventh-generation line from John Alden and Priscilla Mullens of the Mayflower — she of “Speak for yourself, John” — married in the spring of 1621.

Both charts are typed out in full in the book, spelling and all, ending at the same name: the eldest Mulshine daughter. Charlemagne to the Bronx, in one unbroken column of typescript.

The book: the charts pp. 172–176 · also unfolded, entry by entry, in the interactive family tree
IX · Kerry

The Rose of Tralee

“Our most famous Irish relative,” John calls him: William Pembroke Mulchinock, poet, of the same rare Kerry-and-Cork name as the Castletownroche line.

William loved Mary O'Connor, a shoemaker's daughter who worked in his family's house — a match his merchant family would not allow. Accused after a political melee, he fled to India for six years, secretly engaged. He came home to Tralee to marry her, and met a funeral coming down the street. It was hers.

The song he left her — The Rose of Tralee — is still sung, and the festival named for it still crowns a Rose every year, in Tralee and around the world. The book keeps the whole story, and the song's pages besides.

He asked to be buried beside her at Clogherbrien.

The book: the Rose of Tralee story pp. 184–192; the song itself is kept as its pages, pp. 187–190
X · 28 December 1929

Vincent & Dorothy

The two rivers met in the Bronx: Vincent Joseph Mulshine — who had started on the Stock Exchange floor as a twelve-year-old board boy and rose to a Wall Street desk — married Dorothy Marie Haigh, a sometime model, granddaughter of the wire man, carrying the blood of the Mayflower and, so the professor said, of Charlemagne.

Here they are in their bathing suits on the rocks, his arm around her, in the photograph the book keeps.

When Dorothy's father saw the tenement where they were starting out, he gave her eight thousand dollars; they bought the house in Hollis, Queens. Every Christmas, Vincent put a checkerboard, a horn, and a drum under the tree. Seven children came: Doris, Vincent Jr., Maureen, Barbara Ann, Robert, Michael — and John.

“Did you watch my son get his diploma today?” — Dorothy, June 1967, to the teacher who said John would never graduate
The book: Vincent & Dorothy pp. 68–82; the photographs pp. 72–75
XI · Lawn Chairs

The Seven

A summer afternoon in the 1970s: lawn chairs under the trees, tray tables, drinking glasses, a clothesline behind. The back of the photograph names them — John, Michael, Maureen, Dorothy, Vincent; Robert, Doris, Barbara.

Doris the nurse, who sat up with small John the night before his tonsils came out. Michael, “the best of the seven siblings,” who kept everyone in touch. Barbara down the street in Massapequa, married to Jim Murphy, “a classic Irishman....gregarious, sentimental, hot tempered, and warm hearted.”

Sixty-six years to the day after Vincent married Dorothy, John married Patricia — 28 December 1995. Some dates run in families, like names do.

The book: the seven, pp. 69–71; the lawn photograph p. 76
XII · Sláinte

The Man at the Sign

In 1991, John stood at the Castletownroche town sign — the photograph on the cover of his book — and spent a day in Mallow with a florist named Timothy Mulchinock, whose grandfather, of course, was named Moses.

Then he spent thirty years walking his family back through parish registers, ship manifests, censuses, prison records, cemetery maps, and songs — and wrote it all down for his children.

“So, I hope you enjoy learning about the folks who preceded you... This is for you and your children, or grandchildren to add down the road. Sláinte! — Dad” — the letter that opens the book

Prepared with gratitude from the pages of John's book, August 2026 — a thank-you for three days of great hospitality. The full book lives on as a searchable digital edition, and the family as an interactive tree, alongside this story.
